Accordingly, we generated a focused enAsCas12a sgRNA minipool library targeting 250 genes from 9 core functional classes (5 related to adhesion–cytoskeleton, 1 for lipid metabolism and an additional 3 from the 3D versus 2D dependency comparison; Fig. 5c, Extended Data Fig. 9a and Supplementary Table 3). Viability screens using this library were conducted across seven models, testing combinations of growth format (2D plastic or 3D Matrigel dome) and medium type (serum-containing RPMI–FBS or serum-free OPAC) for a total of 18 screens (Extended Data Fig. 9b).
After applying Chronos to the minipool screen data (which correlated well with genome-wide data, r > 0.59; Extended Data Fig. 9c), we used linear regression to distinguish growth-format and culture-medium effects. This analysis identified seven genes for which dependencies were altered by growth formats (q < 0.05), including three integrin subunits (ITGB1, ITGAV and ITGA3) and two actin regulators (NCKAP1 and PTK2; Fig. 5d and Extended Data Fig. 9d). Eight genes also exhibited dependency changes across different media, three of which regulate lipid metabolism (SPTLC1, SPTLC2 and SQLE; Fig. 5e and Extended Data Fig. 9e).
A global analysis of the minipool screen results across the nine functional gene classes did not reveal collective enhancement or impairment of dependencies between different growth formats and media, except for a minor enhancement (Δdependency = 0.09) in the actin regulation class under RPMI–FBS conditions compared with OPAC (Extended Data Fig. 9f,g). To capture opposing effects in gene classes (for example, ITGB1 dependency increases whereas ITGAV decreases in dome culture), we analysed the variance in dependency score differences between conditions (dome versus plastic and OPAC versus RPMI–FBS). Growth format had significantly larger effects on integrin (q = 7.3 × 10−5) and actin regulation genes (q = 7.2 × 10−14), whereas culture medium significantly affected lipid metabolism genes (q = 1.5 × 10−4; Fig. 5f,g). These data demonstrate functional class-specific effects of growth format and medium.
Notably, neither growth format nor medium significantly affected dependencies on the WNT signalling regulators FZD5 and WLS (Fig. 5f), which were essential only in organoids with high PDAC-classical/MUC program levels (Fig. 4f,g). This result probably reflects stable maintenance of the PDAC-classical/MUC program in organoids rather than its rapid induction by the short-term shift in culture conditions. This result is in contrast to integrin, actin and lipid metabolism dependencies, which seem to be more responsive to acute changes in growth conditions. Together, these findings highlight how dependencies on specific cellular processes vary with culture environment and underscore the importance of selecting appropriate model systems for the biological question being pursued.
NextGen models preserve key tumour-relevant transcriptional programs that are lost in traditional cell lines. These include the PDAC-classical/MUC program in gastrointestinal cancer organoids (Fig. 4b,c and Extended Data Fig. 7c) and neural-lineage-specific programs and a glial state in GBM spheroids (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 6a–d). The maintenance of these programs correlated with selective dependencies, which highlights the utility of the NextGen models in identifying certain transcriptional-state-specific vulnerabilities missed by the traditional models.
Our data also revealed that oncogenic signalling roles differ significantly between model types. WNT signalling is required for organoids with a PDAC-classical/MUC program but is largely dispensable in traditional models (Fig. 4). By contrast, dependencies on ESR1 and ERBB2 were exclusive to traditional cell lines (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 5b,d), which probably stem from reduced expression of these oncogenes in the organoids (Extended Data Fig. 5d) owing to composition differences in the media. Together, these findings demonstrate that multiple oncogenic signalling pathways are highly context-dependent, which reinforces the fact that cellular microenvironments substantially shape requirements for these pathways56,57.
Organoid media were prepared using the recommendations provided for each of the models (Supplementary Table 1). The conditioned media were prepared by culturing WNT3A-producing L cells (L Wnt-3A; ATCC, CRL-2647) and R-spondin-1-producing 293T cells (Cultrex R-spondin 1 (RSPO1) cells; Trevigen, 3710-001-K) in DMEM with 10% serum. After reaching 80% confluency, cells were washed once with PBS and incubated with Advanced DMEM–F12 medium (Thermo Fisher, 12634028) containing 100 mM HEPES, 1% penicillin–streptomycin and 1% 100× Glutamax (Ad+++) for another week. The conditioned medium from this culture was then collected, filtered and stored at –80 °C before being used for organoid cultures. All organoids were grown initially as domes composed of 75% growth-factor-reduced, Phenol Red-free Matrigel (50 μl per dome; Corning, 356231) in the recommended medium diluted 1:1 with Ad+++. The screening of organoids was conducted either in Matrigel dome cultures or in adherent cultures on Matrigel-coated plates (see the section ‘Genome-wide CRISPR screening of organoids’ below).
To test whether the observed association between the cancer gene alteration and dependency was consistently beyond the effects caused by lineage bias of the cancer gene alteration, we also computed the differences in mean dependency between NextGen screens in each lineage and the remaining NextGen screens, only considering lineages that have at least five models screened. If the dependency difference observed across the two classes of models distinguished by the presence of a cancer gene alteration was outside the range of all dependency differences observed across all lineages, then we deemed the dependency–biomarker relationship to be driven by the cancer gene alteration. Otherwise, the dependency pattern was attributed to lineage effects. The mean dependency scores for the altered and unaltered groups, as well as the significance of these mean dependency scores, were similarly calculated for all these 6 oncogenes and 13 TSGs in the traditional models (n = 597).
To identify a CN of a gene that can serve as a biomarker to predict CDK6 dependency, the Pearson’s correlation between CDK6 dependency and CN of genes (only those in the top 10% high variance of CN in the DepMap GBM models) was calculated and plotted across DepMap GBM models (with CRISPR and CN data; n = 95; Fig. 3f). The correlation between CDK6 dependency and CN of genes was similarly calculated using only the DepMap GBM models that exhibited the glial pattern of gene expression (n = 36; Extended Data Fig. 6g). Associations with |r | > 0.3 and q < 0.05 were considered as significant. We also analysed the difference in CDK6 dependency between mutant and non-mutant screens for all the hotspot or damaging mutations that have ≥5 mutant cases in the DepMap GBM models (5 mutations met this criterion; Extended Data Fig. 6f) again using the data from the entire DepMap GBM model cohort. None of these mutations was significantly associated with CDK6 dependency (all q > 0.95 by a two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-test).
To assess the relationship between PDAC-classical/MUC program expression and the classical score (based on a previously defined ‘classical’ gene set46) of tumour samples, the classical score was determined using the same strategy as the calculation of the MP expression score described above (in the section ‘Scoring the activity of gene expression MPs’). The relationship between the purity of tumour samples and the level of PDAC-classical/MUC program expression was analysed by compiling the ABSOLUTE tumour purity score of the TCGA tumour samples of pancreas, oesophagus–stomach and colorectal lineages (n = 149, 375 and 448, respectively) from previous studies59,73.
The expression levels of the PDAC-classical/MUC program in various sample types (tumours, NextGen models and traditional cell lines) were also visualized by the colour of the points on the Celligner plots (Fig. 4c and Extended Data Fig. 7c) to show the similarity of the overall gene expression profiles of the models and tumours displaying high expression levels of this program across different lineages (pancreas, oesophagus–stomach and colorectal).
To identify genetic dependencies associated with the level of PDAC-classical/MUC program expression, the Pearson’s correlation coefficient and the significance of correlation (two-tailed) were calculated between the level of the PDAC-classical/MUC program and the dependency scores of strong dependency genes (strongly selective + high variance + pan-dependency; n = 3,521) identified from the organoid screen data using all the organoid models with gene expression and CRISPR screen data (n = 108 (all organoids), n = 60 (organoids grown with R-spondin 1 and WNT3A); Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 7i). The enrichment of the MSigDB gene set ‘GOBP WNT signalling pathway’ in the dependencies associated with PDAC-classical/MUC program expression was assessed by gene set enrichment analysis, which was conducted using the open-source code GSEApy (v.1.1.5; https://pypi.org/project/gseapy/) (Fig. 4d).
The PDAC-classical/MUC program-associated dependencies on the selective components of the WNT signalling pathway, namely TCF7L2, WLS, FZD5 and MESD (plus LGR4 for some analyses), were investigated further as follows. The dependency on these WNT pathway components were compared between the organoid models (n = 108) and the traditional cell lines that have lineage-matched organoid models (screen n = 485) using the density plots and two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests (Fig. 4f). To test whether dependencies on these WNT pathway components observed in organoids (with high levels of PDAC-classical/MUC program expression) is driven by specific mutations, 14 hotspot mutations and 573 damaging mutations that have 2 or more mutant models in the cohort of CRISPR-screened organoids (n = 108) were selected. For each of these 587 mutation types, dependencies on the 5 WNT pathway components listed above were compared between the mutant and non-mutant models (Extended Data Fig. 7k). For mutations and CN alterations that result in the activation of the WNT pathway, namely, APC damaging mutation, CTNNB1 hotspot mutation, CTNNB1 CN amplification and RNF43 damaging mutation, dependencies on TCF7L2, WLS, FZD5 and MESD were also compared between the organoids that have at least one of these alterations (n = 30) and those that do not have any of them (n = 78) (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b).
For the minipool screens, to evaluate the effects of growth formats and culture media on gene essentiality, we decided to select test genes from nine different functional classes. Most of these gene classes are related to the regulation of adhesion–cytoskeleton, lipid metabolism or other processes highlighted in the systematic comparison of genome-wide CRISPR screen data between 2D models and 3D organoids (Fig. 5a,b). The following gene classes were included: integrin (genes encoding an integrin α or β subunit); ECM adhesion (adhesome, https://adhesome.org/); actin regulation (MSigDB gene set and KEGG regulation of actin cytoskeleton); adherens junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG adherens junction); tight junction (MSigDB gene set and KEGG tight junction); lipid metabolism (a union of two MSigDB gene sets, Hallmark cholesterol homeostasis and Reactome metabolism of lipids); WNT signalling (MSigDB gene set and GOBP WNT signalling pathway); PI3K–mTOR signalling (MSigDB gene set and Hallmark PI3K–mTOR signalling); cell cycle (MSigDB gene set and GOBP cell cycle); and other genes of particular interest (manual curation). To select 250 test genes from these 9 core functional gene classes, we used the dependency profiles of the gene between 2D models and 3D organoids to prioritize genes that exhibited selective enrichment of dependency in either of these model types. Many of these test genes belong to multiple different classes, and the patterns of membership of individual genes across the nine classes and the number of test genes that exhibit the specific pattern are presented in Extended Data Fig. 9a. We then added 650 non-dependency genes and 100 pan-dependency genes, genes that are universally essential across 2D models and 3D organoids, to compile a list of 1,000 genes (Supplementary Table 3). We subsequently designed 4 enAsCas12a sgRNA sequences for each of these 1,000 genes using the CRISPick web tool (https://portals.broadinstitute.org/gppx/crispick/public), which were assembled into 2 constructs (2 sgRNA sequences for the same gene per construct; 2 constructs per gene) of the pRDA_052 backbone (Addgene, 136474). The resulting library with 2,000 constructs was used for minipool screening.
Minipool screens were evaluated for sequencing quality by having a total read count of at least 500,000 reads across replicates. Gene scores and NNMDs were computed in the same manner as the genome-wide screens. Replicate correlation was computed as the Pearson’s correlation coefficient over log fold changes in all non-control genes. Screens with NNMDs greater than –1.5 and replicate correlations less than 0.2 were excluded from downstream analyses. Screens with a single replicate were retained if their other metrics passed these quality control thresholds. Chronos scores were calculated as previously described23, with adjusted hyperparameters (smoothing regularization parameter = 0.3, kernel width = 5) for the smaller library size. The number of screens for each condition is as follows: dome format, n = 11; plastic format, n = 7; OPAC medium, n = 9; RPMI–FBS medium, n = 9.
For Fig. 5g, the variances of dependency between different growth formats and different culture media were scored for all nine of the core functional classes of minipool target genes. The variances were compared between in-class genes and out-of-class genes (that is, rest of the 250 test genes in the minipool library) for each of the 9 core functional classes using one-tailed F-tests. The functional class is considered to be significantly affected by the growth format or culture medium if the corresponding q value was less than 0.05. The numbers of genes in each of the 9 core functional classes are as follows: actin regulation, n = 75; adherens junction, n = 30; cell cycle, n = 53; ECM adhesion, n = 89; integrin, n = 22; lipid metabolism, n = 20; PI3K–mTOR signalling, n = 20; tight junction, n = 34; WNT signalling, n = 29.
For Extended Data Fig. 7d, the expression scores of the PDAC-classical/MUC program were compared between the oesophageal squamous adenocarcinoma subtype and other subtypes of the TCGA oesophagus–stomach tumour samples using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests. The number of tumour samples in each of the subtypes of TCGA oesophagus–stomach tumour subtypes are as follows: all oesophagus–stomach tumours, n = 602; diffuse-type stomach adenocarcinoma, n = 68; oesophageal adenocarcinoma, n = 89; oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, n = 92; gastrointestinal stromal tumour, n = 6; intestinal-type stomach adenocarcinoma, n = 72; mucinous stomach adenocarcinoma, n = 20; papillary stomach adenocarcinoma, n = 7; signet ring cell carcinoma of the stomach, n = 12; stomach adenocarcinoma, n = 159; and tubular stomach adenocarcinoma, n = 76.

The number of remaining samples in each class is as follows: TCGA tumours, n = 510; NextGen models, n = 86; and traditional models, n = 52.
For Extended Data Fig. 7f, Pearson’s correlation of previously published classical scores46 and previously defined PDAC-classical/MUC scores37 across the cohort of TCGA-plus solid tumour samples (n = 11,029) was calculated.
For Extended Data Fig. 7h, Pearson’s correlation of ABSOLUTE tumour purity score and the PDAC-classical/MUC score was calculated individually for TCGA-plus tumours of colorectal (n = 375), oesophagus–stomach (n = 448) and pancreas (n = 149) lineages.
For Extended Data Fig. 7i, Pearson’s correlation between the gene dependency and expression score of the PDAC-classical/MUC program across the organoid models that were propagated in the presence of R-spondin 1 and WNT3A ligands (gene n = 3,521 (strong dependency in organoids), model n = 60) was calculated for identifying dependencies associated with the expression of this program.
For Extended Data Fig. 7k, for each of the hotspot and damaging mutations that have ≥2 mutated organoids (with CRISPR screen data; n = 108 (model), 587 (mutation)), dependencies on the five regulators of WNT signalling, including MESD, WLS, TCF7L2, FZD5 and LGR4, were compared between the non-mutated and mutated organoids using two-tailed Mann–Whitney U-tests.

For Extended Data Fig. 9d,e, for the seven pairs of minipool screens that were conducted with the same model, same medium but different growth format (dome versus plastic), the Chronos dependency scores of all the test genes in the minipool library (n = 250) were compared using two-tailed paired t-tests (d). Extended Data Fig. 5Dependencies linked to gene expression identified in NextGen vs traditional models.a, Representative distribution of dependency scores for each dependency category. Each gene evaluated by the CRISPR screen was classified into either of these five dependency classes based on the distribution of its Chronos dependency scores across DepMap NextGen models (or organoid models). We used a previously published strategy for this classification25 (also see Methods). b, Correlation of expression and dependency for PROX1 and ERBB2 in the NextGen (left) and traditional (right) models. Elevated expression of PROX1 correlated with enhanced dependency on its own more strongly in the NextGen models (r = −0.462) than in the traditional cell lines (r = −0.182). In contrast, while the traditional cell lines exhibit very strong association (r = −0.530) between the expression and dependency levels of ERBB2, this relationship was much weaker (r = −0.077) in the NextGen models. Here and in e, regression lines with 95% confidence intervals are displayed. c, Increased expression of HNRNPH1 and PROX1 and reduced expression of ENO2 in tumors relative to lineage-matched normal tissues. The expression levels of HNRNPH1, PROX1 and ENO2 in the tumor tissues and corresponding normal tissues were analyzed per lineage in the combined TCGA/TARGET/GTEx dataset downloaded from the Xena browser (https://xenabrowser.net/). n = 9 (biliary tract, normal), 36 (biliary tract, tumor), 1,151 (CNS-brain, normal), 689 (CNS-brain, tumor), 355 (colorectal, normal), 383 (colorectal, tumor), 152 (prostate, normal), and 496 (prostate, tumor). Expression values were plotted for the lineages with tumor-specific upregulation (HNRNPH1 and PROX1) or downregulation (ENO2) of these genes. The centre line and box denote median and 25th to 75th percentile data points, respectively, and whiskers extend up to 1.5 times the interquartile range from box edges. P-values were scored by two-tailed Mann-Whitney U test. d, Reduced expression of ESR1/ERBB2 underlies the absence of expression addiction for these oncogenes in the NextGen breast cancer models. The association between the expression and dependency of two breast cancer oncogenes, ESR1 and ERBB2, was plotted for the NextGen (green circles) and traditional (navy circles) breast cancer models. None of the 14 breast cancer organoids exhibited high (log2[TPM + 1] > 3.4) expression of ESR1, while 11 out of the 51 traditional breast cancer models showed high expression of this oncogene. All the traditional cell lines with strong (Chronos score < −1) ESR1 dependency displayed high expression of ESR1. ELMO2 dependency was correlated strongly (r = 0.545) with reduced expression of its paralog ELMO3 in the traditional cell lines, while this relationship was not observed (r = −0.110) in the NextGen models.

To gain insights into the underlying mechanisms of these differential dependencies, we used linear regression models to link gene fitness effects with our curated genomic, patient and clinical features. From this analysis, we identified 1,841 significant gene–biomarker associations (based on false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted P values and effect size; Extended Data Fig. 9d and Supplementary Table 8), distributed across categories of genetic constraint (Fig. 4f, labelled A, B or C depending on strength of statistical association). In COAD/READ, we observed dependency on WRN associated with a RNF43 mutation (effect size = −0.747, adjusted P value = 0.01), RPL22 or SETD1B mutations (effect size = −0.641, adjusted P value = 0.027) and mutational signature SBS44 (effect size = −0.823, adjusted P value = 0.0009), consistent with MSI status due to deficient DNA mismatch repair (Extended Data Fig. 9e) and showcasing the value of integrating multi-omics biomarkers. Notably, four MSI organoids were not WRN-dependent, and lacked expanded TA dinucleotide repeats associated with deficient DNA mismatch repair and underlying WRN dependency and inhibitor sensitivity49, showing the utility of a large biobank to sub-stratify responses.
We also identified MDM2 dependency for TP53-wild-type (effect size = 0.463, adjusted P value = 0.001) and unexpectedly for KRASG12D COAD/READ organoids (effect size = −0.576, adjusted P value = 0.01), of which 4 out of 5 were TP53-wild-type. HRAS gain-of-function events (effect size = −0.829, adjusted P value = 0.0019) partially mirrored MDM2 gain-of-function events (effect size = −0.566, adjusted P value = 0.0039), and all of them correlating with sensitivity to nutlin-3a (an MDM2 inhibitor, PCC = 0.49) (Extended Data Fig. 9f). For ESCA, CCNE1 amplification, which occurs in 7% of patients50, was associated with dependency on CCNE1 (effect size = −0.645, adjusted P value = 3.65 × 10−5) (Extended Data Fig. 9g). Across gastrointestinal organoids, INTS6L expression correlates with INTS6 dependency (effect size = 2.229, adjusted P value = 5.28 × 10−15) (Extended Data Fig. 9h), as previously described in cell lines51. This rich landscape of dependency–biomarker associations illustrates the value of integrating genomic, transcriptomic and clinical features, and highlights novel hypotheses for functional investigation. Some biomarker-linked differential dependencies map to genes under low genetic constraint (Fig. 4f), which may render them suitable candidate therapeutic targets.
To identify molecular and clinical features associated with context-specific gene dependencies, we performed a systematic biomarker analysis across gastrointestinal, COAD/READ and ESCA organoids. Candidate dependencies were selected from the differential dependency analysis based on recurrence criteria and evaluated against a curated set of genomic, transcriptomic and clinical features, including driver mutations and specific variants, copy number alterations, structural events, mutational signatures, gene expression, pathway activity scores, and composite loss- and gain-of-function events. Associations between gene fitness effects and features were tested using linear regression models incorporating relevant technical and biological covariates, with significance assessed using likelihood-ratio tests and multiple testing correction. Significant associations were prioritized based on adjusted P value and effect size and classified into tiers reflecting strength of association. Full details of feature selection, model specification, statistical thresholds and classification criteria are provided in the Supplementary Information.

These MPs represent recurrent gene expression modules that account for intratumour heterogeneity (Fig. 3a) and largely reflect environmentally driven gene expression changes. GENES ['CDK4', 'CDK6'] TEXT Next, we explored vulnerabilities tied to glial gene expression. We identified an enrichment of CDK6 dependency in glial compared with mesenchymal models (Δdependency = –0.44, P = 0.013) (Fig. 3d,e). Although this dependency ranked second in effect size, it fell short of the multiple-testing significance threshold (q = 0.28), which may be due to the small sample size of glial GBMs (n = 36) analysed. Comparisons with other NextGen models confirmed that this enrichment was driven by the glial state rather than serum-free media (Fig. 3e and Extended Data Fig. 6e). Encouraged by the clinical impact of CDK4 and CDK6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors on treatment outcomes, we pursued CDK6 dependency and its associated biomarker.
GENES ['CDK6'] TEXT Although no recurrent GBM mutations correlated closely with CDK6 dependency (Extended Data Fig. 6f), significant associations were found with CNs of genes, including those on chromosome 9p21.3 (Fig. 3f). Of these genes, CDKN2A—which encodes p16INK4A and is the most frequently deleted gene in GBM41—exhibited the third strongest correlation with CDK6 dependency across adult GBM models (r = 0.520, q = 4.12 × 10−5) and the strongest in glial GBM models specifically (r = 0.640, q = 0.0340; Extended Data Fig. 6g). Given the established role of CDKN2A in CDK6-mediated cell cycle control, we postulated that CDKN2A CN loss is a biomarker for CDK6 dependency in glial GBM.
GENES ['CDK4', 'CDK6'] TEXT Validation with individual sgRNAs confirmed that CDK6 knockout caused greater viability loss than CDK4 knockout in two glial GBM models with CDKN2A loss (Extended Data Fig. 6h,i). This result is consistent with the reported exclusive CDK6 dependency in GBM stem cells with CDKN2A and CDKN2B loss42. Glial models with CDKN2A loss were also significantly more sensitive to CDK6 depletion than mesenchymal models with the same deletion (Fig. 3g). This finding indicates that glial gene expression and CDKN2A loss independently contribute to CDK6 dependency.
GENES ['CDK4'] TEXT To pharmacologically validate this association, we profiled seven glial GBM models—five with CDKN2A CN loss and two CN neutral—against three CDK4/6 inhibitors (abemaciclib, palbociclib and ribociclib) using the dye drop method43. CDKN2A CN-loss models were more sensitive (mean growth rate AOC (GRAOC) = 0.35, 0.25 and 0.15, respectively) to all three inhibitors than CN-neutral models (GRAOC = 0.06, –0.03 and –0.07, respectively), with significant differences for abemaciclib (P = 7.1 × 10−4) and palbociclib (P = 0.021) (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 6j). CN-loss models also displayed reductions in the S phase fraction at doses that did not affect CN-neutral models (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 6k), which—together with a previous report on CRISPR-mediated CDKN2A depletion44—provides support for a causal role of CDKN2A loss in enhancing CDK4/6 inhibitor sensitivity.
GENES ['CDK4', 'CDK6'] TEXT In summary, CDKN2A loss increases CDK6 dependency and CDK4/6 inhibitor sensitivity in glial GBM. Given that 92% of glial and classical GBM tumours exhibit homozygous 9p21.3 deletion45, these findings indicate that CDK6 inhibition is a relevant therapeutic strategy. These results also underscore the value of NextGen CNS models in uncovering clinically relevant vulnerabilities because they preserve tumour transcriptional states.

GENES ['CTNNB1', 'FZD5', 'TCF7L2', 'WLS'] TEXT To identify dependencies associated with this program, we correlated PDAC-classical/MUC scores with dependency scores of strong dependency genes (3 strong dependency classes in organoids; n = 3,521). The top correlated dependencies were enriched for canonical WNT signalling regulators, including MESD (ranked first; r = −0.544), WLS (second; r = −0.507), TCF7L2 (fifth; r = −0.454), FZD5 (seventh; r = −0.435) and LGR4 (21st; r = −0.354) (Fig. 4d,e). This association held when restricting the analysis to organoids grown with R-spondin 1 and WNT3A (Extended Data Fig. 7i), which indicated that it was not driven solely by the presence of WNT activators in culture media. Notably, other WNT regulators (for example, CTNNB1 and BCL9L) did not correlate significantly (Fig. 4d and Extended Data Fig. 7j), which suggests that the association is limited to selective WNT signalling components.
GENES ['APC', 'CTNNB1'] TEXT A similar WNT pathway dependency is known in traditional PDAC models with RNF43 LOF49. However, in organoids, these dependencies correlated with the PDAC-classical/MUC transcriptional state irrespective of RNF43, APC, CTNNB1 or AXIN2 mutations (Extended Data Figs. 7k and 8a,b). All 19 organoids strongly dependent on the five listed WNT regulators (average Chronos dependency score < –1) were PDAC-classical/MUC-high (expression score > 2.8), including those with and without WNT-activating genetic alterations (Extended Data Fig. 8b). This result suggests that enhanced WNT dependency is driven by the transcriptional cell state rather than genetic alterations.
GENES ['FZD5', 'TCF7L2', 'WLS'] TEXT These findings extend previous work on the loss of WNT3A and R-spondin dependence during PDAC organoid niche-adaptation50 by linking specific WNT signalling dependencies to a conserved mucinous differentiation program active across multiple gastrointestinal tumour types. The expression of this program in a subset of lung and cervix tumours suggests a shared WNT-associated vulnerability in these rare, poor-prognosis cancers51,52. Notably, MESD, WLS, TCF7L2 and FZD5 dependencies were significantly weaker in lineage-matched 2D models (P < 4 × 10−12 for all; Fig. 4f,g and Extended Data Fig. 8c), which provides further support that the PDAC-classical/MUC program, maintained only in organoids, drives these dependencies.
GENES ['FZD5', 'WLS'] TEXT Notably, neither growth format nor medium significantly affected dependencies on the WNT signalling regulators FZD5 and WLS (Fig. 5f), which were essential only in organoids with high PDAC-classical/MUC program levels (Fig. 4f,g). This result probably reflects stable maintenance of the PDAC-classical/MUC program in organoids rather than its rapid induction by the short-term shift in culture conditions. This result is in contrast to integrin, actin and lipid metabolism dependencies, which seem to be more responsive to acute changes in growth conditions. Together, these findings highlight how dependencies on specific cellular processes vary with culture environment and underscore the importance of selecting appropriate model systems for the biological question being pursued.
GENES ['ERBB2'] TEXT Our data also revealed that oncogenic signalling roles differ significantly between model types. WNT signalling is required for organoids with a PDAC-classical/MUC program but is largely dispensable in traditional models (Fig. 4). By contrast, dependencies on ESR1 and ERBB2 were exclusive to traditional cell lines (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 5b,d), which probably stem from reduced expression of these oncogenes in the organoids (Extended Data Fig. 5d) owing to composition differences in the media. Together, these findings demonstrate that multiple oncogenic signalling pathways are highly context-dependent, which reinforces the fact that cellular microenvironments substantially shape requirements for these pathways56,57.
GENES ['CDK6'] TEXT To identify a CN of a gene that can serve as a biomarker to predict CDK6 dependency, the Pearson’s correlation between CDK6 dependency and CN of genes (only those in the top 10% high variance of CN in the DepMap GBM models) was calculated and plotted across DepMap GBM models (with CRISPR and CN data; n = 95; Fig. 3f). The correlation between CDK6 dependency and CN of genes was similarly calculated using only the DepMap GBM models that exhibited the glial pattern of gene expression (n = 36; Extended Data Fig. 6g). Associations with |r | > 0.3 and q < 0.05 were considered as significant. line 4 Although no recurrent GBM mutations correlated closely with CDK6 dependency (Extended Data Fig. 6f), significant associations were found with CNs of genes, including those on chromosome 9p21.3 (Fig. 3f). Of these genes, CDKN2A—which encodes p16INK4A and is the most frequently deleted gene in GBM41—exhibited the third strongest correlation with CDK6 dependency across adult GBM models (r = 0.520, q = 4.12 × 10−5) and the strongest in glial GBM models specifically (r = 0.640, q = 0.0340; Extended Data Fig. 6g). Given the established role of CDKN2A in CDK6-mediated cell cycle control, we postulated that CDKN2A CN loss is a biomarker for CDK6 dependency in glial GBM.
line 4 Validation with individual sgRNAs confirmed that CDK6 knockout caused greater viability loss than CDK4 knockout in two glial GBM models with CDKN2A loss (Extended Data Fig. 6h,i). This result is consistent with the reported exclusive CDK6 dependency in GBM stem cells with CDKN2A and CDKN2B loss42. Glial models with CDKN2A loss were also significantly more sensitive to CDK6 depletion than mesenchymal models with the same deletion (Fig. 3g). This finding indicates that glial gene expression and CDKN2A loss independently contribute to CDK6 dependency.
line 4 Our data also revealed that oncogenic signalling roles differ significantly between model types. WNT signalling is required for organoids with a PDAC-classical/MUC program but is largely dispensable in traditional models (Fig. 4). By contrast, dependencies on ESR1 and ERBB2 were exclusive to traditional cell lines (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 5b,d), which probably stem from reduced expression of these oncogenes in the organoids (Extended Data Fig. 5d) owing to composition differences in the media. Together, these findings demonstrate that multiple oncogenic signalling pathways are highly context-dependent, which reinforces the fact that cellular microenvironments substantially shape requirements for these pathways56,57.

The second and third terms capture the growth format effect and medium effect, where Id and Is are indicator variables representing the types of growth format (Matrigel dome culture (dome) versus monolayer culture on plastic plates (plastic)) and culture medium (serum-free OPAC medium versus serum-containing RPMI–FBS medium), respectively. The fourth term captures interaction effects between these two conditions, and the final term captures model effects to account for multiple screens in the same cell line. Differences in effect sizes across growth format and serum status were extracted as βd and βs, respectively. Significance values corresponding to the same coefficients were extracted from the P values calculated using two-sided linear regression t-test.

item.text:
The package needs further fixes before a ≥90 integrity score. I found two high-severity issues and no critical issues. The scientific result remains a candidate bound; this review grants no scientific gate.

Paths below are relative to `cancer-dependency-rsi/`, except root `PLAN.md` and `GOAL.md`.

1. **HIGH — C7 annotations still omit known findings and contain false “not located” dispositions.**  
   Evidence: `src/build_atlas_v3.py:50–56`; `atlas/v3/genes.csv:35,93,231,250`; `atlas/v3/manifest.json:24–25`. CDK6 receives an S3 transfer annotation but omits S1’s CDKN2A-copy-loss/glial-state biomarker evidence, explicitly reported in cached `data/papers/PMC13581591.xml:4`, Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6. FZD5/TCF7L2/WLS receive state-association tags while their biomarker dispositions say no gene-specific report was located. Moreover, 234 genes say “author_library_class_only_no_gene_specific_S1_report_located” despite having joined author-test results. The inherited `prior_knowledge_status` also remains generic throughout.  
   **Exact fix:** annotate S1’s CDK6 findings with their distinct significance qualifications; classify the WNT state associations consistently across prior and biomarker fields; distinguish “tested, not FDR-significant” from “not assessed/not located”; reconcile obsolete status fields and manifest descriptions. Add regression assertions for these known cases.

2. **HIGH — pgen001’s required pre-run ledger lock is not witnessed.**  
   Evidence: root `PLAN.md:72` requires the SPEC hash locked **in the ledger before any run**; `generations/pgen001/SPEC.md:9` asserts prospective freezing. The only pgen001 ledger entry is the completed screen at `ledger/experiments.jsonl:31`. `GENERATIONS.md:4` nevertheless claims the hash was locked before probing. The current SPEC hash matches, but that establishes current content, not prospective locking. A generation-specific reserved battery budget is also absent.  
   **Exact fix:** retain contemporaneous evidence establishing the original SPEC/hash and probe chronology, and append an honest reconciliation. If that evidence cannot establish prospective locking, label pgen001 exploratory/protocol-deviating and run any subsequent screen under a new version with its hash and battery reservation ledgered beforehand. Do not backdate a lock.

3. **MEDIUM — `SCREEN-POSITIVE_CONDITIONAL` does not meet the frozen screen bar.**  
   Evidence: `generations/pgen001/SPEC.md:19–25`; `screen_results_v1.json:3–6`; `token_accounting_audit.json:11`. The SPEC requires a conservative **predeclared** failure charge. The results explicitly defer that rule to a future Lock-1 draft. Criterion 2 also requires licenses and remaining-allowance verification, neither demonstrated by the supplied screen artifacts.  
   **Exact fix:** preserve v1 and issue a versioned disposition of `PENDING` or `FAILS-SCREEN`, listing the unmet conditions. A revised screen must prospectively specify a demonstrably conservative failure-charge rule and document every required route condition before declaring passage.

4. **MEDIUM — Metadata acquisition and non-exposure claims lack an auditable request trail.**  
   Evidence: `screen_results_v1.json:5–7`; `ledger/experiments.jsonl:31`; `raw_counts_zip_listing.json:1`. The listing retains filenames and sizes, but no request ranges, response headers, source receipt, request/byte/time totals, or reproducible extraction procedure. The Passports probe remains described as an unmanifested `/tmp` artifact. Consequently, the HEAD checksum, metadata counts, budget compliance and metadata-only acquisition cannot all be independently verified from this package.  
   **Exact fix:** retain or recover contemporaneous request receipts, exact ranges, response headers, acquisition code, hashes, license evidence, metadata snapshot and cumulative budget accounting. Record unsupported historical assertions as unverified where recovery is impossible.

5. **MEDIUM — The novelty repair is substantively correct, but the mandated search completion remains unwitnessed.**  
   Evidence: root `PLAN.md:174`; `reviews/novelty_audit_v4.md:17–29`; previous review `reviews/sci_package_high_review_v1.md:7`. V4 documents S1/S3 identifier searches, but no corresponding S2 check, systematic backward/forward citation checks, or completion of the requested broader full-text/preprint and closest supplement/code checks. “Retained in session record” provides no resolvable package reference.  
   **Exact fix:** retain dated queries, source identifiers, returned records and screening dispositions; complete the missing checks or explicitly mark them outstanding. Keep C1/C6 partial until that evidence is adjudicated.

6. **MEDIUM — pgen001 improperly narrows family reopening after a failed screen.**  
   Evidence: `generations/pgen001/SPEC.md:24–25`, versus root `PLAN.md:81`, `reviews/cl_rd_raw_accounting_discriminator_v2.json:5–9`, and `cancer_rsi_handoff.txt:319`. Its failure rule permits reopening only through user-supplied measured expenditure, excluding justified alternatives and implying family closure without a necessary-condition argument.  
   **Exact fix:** preserve the frozen SPEC and append a correction limiting failure to the tested specification. Keep other alternatives open under discriminator v2 and handoff §11; require a new prospective SPEC for another test.

7. **LOW — The corrected S3 account cites the wrong results section.**  
   Evidence: `reviews/novelty_audit_v4.md:13,21`. Cached `data/papers/PMC13664187.xml:1` places within-organoid ranking in §2.10.1 and §3.7, Tables S17–S19. §3.5/Fig. 6 concerns cross-cohort target-wise synthesis.  
   **Exact fix:** replace those section references with §2.10.1/§3.7 and Tables S17–S19.

8. **LOW — The advertised live checkpoint remains stale.**  
   Evidence: root `PLAN.md:3` and `GOAL.md:79` direct readers to live status, but `status.json:36,103` still records C10 as partial and proposes atlas v2; `STATUS.md:119` still says C was not consumed.  
   **Exact fix:** update `status.json` and append a current `STATUS.md` checkpoint reflecting the executed external test, current artifacts and latest adjudications, while retaining historical entries.

Independent checks that passed:

- The goal objective matches the archived v1 objective verbatim. The v3 notes preserve the joint objective and `COMPLETE_*` requirements.
- S3’s substantive misrepresentation is repaired. Residual novelty is honestly limited to the joined measured-lability/displacement relationship. P3’s drug-response exclusion and P5’s adjacent-context disposition are supported by their abstracts ([P3](https://doi.org/10.1093/bib/bbag559), [P5](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S193459092500298X)).
- All 250 atlas coefficient/FDR joins match the author files. Format FDR<0.05: **CTNNA1, ITGA3, ITGAV, ITGB1, NCKAP1, PRKCA, PTK2**. Serum: **CTNNA1, PPP1R15B, PPP2R2D, PTK2, RICTOR, SPTLC1, SPTLC2, SQLE**. Declared input/code hashes match; inherited values are unchanged; 43 exclusions remain.
- Receipt totals reproduce exactly: 15 completed calls, four without usage; input **8,750,313**, cached input **7,932,416**, output **108,308**, reasoning output **48,689**. These overlapping categories must not simply be added together.
- ZIP metadata contains **1,122** count files, three directory entries and **358** filename prefixes. ZIP-expanded member sizes sum to **2,847,239,686 bytes**; these members remain gzip-compressed.
- The measured-token proposal is explicitly unadjudicated. Discriminator v2 permits feasibility reassessment without granting C9.
- The updated CLI assertion remains a real refusal smoke test: it requires nonzero exit plus a named barrier. I did not execute it because its production launcher can write resource records. The atlas test and lineage validation test passed through direct invocation.

No files were modified or dependency data downloaded. I accessed only permitted reported outcomes. For pgen001, I found no retained evidence of count-value access; the missing acquisition receipts prevent a definitive independent non-exposure certification.

V3_PACKAGE_REVIEW_SCORE: 84; C1:PARTIAL; C6:PARTIAL; C7:PARTIAL; PGEN001:PENDING_NOT_SCREEN_PASSED
